note: The standard multimodal survey, covering architecture, training strategy, hallucination and evaluation.
title: A survey on multimodal large language models

reading.body:
Multimodal large language models combine text processing with image understanding and other input types, rapidly closing the gap with leading proprietary systems while facing persistent challenges like hallucination that currently limit deployment.

The survey documents how these systems work, how they are trained, and where they fail. It covers architectural choices for connecting different input types to a language model foundation, training strategies that leverage existing text models, and evaluation methods still being developed. The core insight is that multimodal capability is being added to language models incrementally rather than built from scratch, making it accessible to more research groups and organizations.

For AI infrastructure, this matters because multimodal systems require the same computational resources as their text-only predecessors, plus additional training data and engineering to handle images and other modalities. The hallucination problem and evaluation gaps the survey identifies are not primarily compute problems. They are architectural and methodological problems that faster chips alone cannot solve. Organizations planning AI infrastructure should recognize that capability is advancing rapidly across both academic and commercial research, but deployment readiness depends on solving these quality and safety challenges.

The survey does not cover which specific systems are most power-efficient to run, how much additional infrastructure multimodal capabilities actually demand compared to text-only models, or whether the data required for training represents a distinct constraint on scaling.

explain_beginner: As language models learned to read and write text extremely well, researchers began asking whether the same core model could also be taught to see, meaning take in an image alongside text and reason about both together, without training an entirely separate system from scratch. Yin and coauthors surveyed this fast growing area, called multimodal large language models, cataloging how systems like GPT-4V and open alternatives such as LLaVA and BLIP-2 are typically built and trained. They describe a common recipe, a pretrained image or audio encoder is connected to a pretrained language model through a lightweight connector, then the combined system is trained in stages, first to align the image and text representations, then to follow instructions, then to match human preferences. The survey found that despite fast progress, these systems still confidently describe things that are not actually in the image, a problem called multimodal hallucination, and that most systems remain heavily English centric and limited to whole image understanding rather than fine grained regions or pixels, gaps the field has not yet closed.
explain_business: The strategic read for a business evaluating multimodal AI, models that can process images and documents together with text, is that the underlying architecture pattern, encoder plus connector plus language model, trained in alignment then instruction then preference stages, has converged across both proprietary systems like GPT-4V and open alternatives, which means switching cost between multimodal vendors is likely to keep falling as the open ecosystem catches up. The unresolved gaps the survey documents are directly relevant to deployment risk, multimodal hallucination means a system can misdescribe an uploaded image or document with full confidence, which matters for any workflow, like compliance review or medical imaging triage, where an incorrect visual claim has real consequences, and the English centric training data means non-English visual and text tasks are likely to underperform benchmarks reported in English. Neither gap is close to resolved as of this survey, so human review remains necessary for any high stakes multimodal deployment today.
explain_practitioner: This survey formalizes multimodal large language models as three connected components, a frozen or lightly tuned modality encoder for images, audio, or video, a large language model that does the actual reasoning, and a modality interface connecting them, using either token level fusion, where visual features become extra input tokens, or feature level fusion, where cross attention modules are inserted inside the language model. Training follows three stages the authors document across dozens of surveyed systems, pretraining for cross modal alignment on caption style data, instruction tuning on formatted task data, and alignment tuning using RLHF or DPO to match human preferences, echoing the pipeline used for text only models but applied across modalities. Rather than one benchmark score, the paper's evidence is its systematic coverage of the field's emergent behaviors, in context learning and chain of thought reasoning extended into the visual domain, and its documentation of unresolved technical gaps, multimodal hallucination, limited support for fine grained spatial or pixel level grounding, and a training and evaluation ecosystem still concentrated in English.
